\chapter{Animals}
\label{ch:sa-animals}
\hlchaptermodality{39}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a cow, a bird, a fish, a dog and a snake in Sanskrit.}

\section[dhenuḥ]{\sk{धेनुः} (dhenuḥ) — a cow}

\label{lesson:SA-C39-cow}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{mṛttikā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{धेनुः}}
\textbf{\sk{धेनुः}} (\emph{dhenuḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a cow\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{धेनुः}} is a cow, and first of all a cow in milk.

It stands on \emph{dhe}, \textquotedblleft{}to suckle\textquotedblright{} — a root that reaches a long way west: Latin \emph{fēmina}, the one who nurses, and \emph{fīlius}, the one nursed, and English \emph{fecund} behind them both.

\sk{दुग्धम्}, the milk you already ask for, comes from a different root altogether, the one that means to draw milk off. The animal is named for the giving, the drink for the taking.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The animal behind the milk word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dhenuḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{mṛttikā}, then \emph{dhenuḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{धेनुः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a cow\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vihagaḥ]{\sk{विहगः} (vihagaḥ) — a bird}

\label{lesson:SA-C39-bird}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{dhenuḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{विहगः}}
\textbf{\sk{विहगः}} (\emph{vihagaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a bird\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{विहगः}} is a bird, and the word says how it moves: \emph{vi-}, \textquotedblleft{}apart, across\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{ga}, \textquotedblleft{}going\textquotedblright{}.

That going-piece is the one inside \sk{गच्छति}, the first doing-word in this book. A \textbf{\sk{विहगः}} is simply the one that goes across.

Across what is unsaid, and does not need saying: \sk{आकाशः}, the open sky, is the only place it could be.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A bird named for crossing the sky.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vihagaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dhenuḥ}, then \emph{vihagaḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{विहगः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a bird\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[matsyaḥ]{\sk{मत्स्यः} (matsyaḥ) — a fish}

\label{lesson:SA-C39-fish}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{vihagaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मत्स्यः}}
\textbf{\sk{मत्स्यः}} (\emph{matsyaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a fish\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{मत्स्यः}} is a fish, in a \sk{नदी} or in a market basket.

It wore down eastward into \emph{machh}, which is why the fish on a Hindi menu is \emph{machhlī} and the Bengali one is \emph{machh}.

Westward there is nothing to point at: no agreed European cousin has been found. A fish seems to be one of the things each family named for itself.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A fish, and a word that travelled east but not west.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{matsyaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vihagaḥ}, then \emph{matsyaḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{मत्स्यः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a fish\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śunakaḥ]{\sk{शुनकः} (śunakaḥ) — a dog}

\label{lesson:SA-C39-dog}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{matsyaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{शुनकः}}
\textbf{\sk{शुनकः}} (\emph{śunakaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a dog\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{शुनकः}} is a dog — an affectionate little form of an older and much bigger word, \emph{śvan}.

That \emph{śvan} is one of the unbroken ones. Greek \emph{kuōn} is behind \emph{cynic}; Latin \emph{canis} is behind \emph{canine} and \emph{kennel}; English \emph{hound} and German \emph{Hund} are the same word worn down the Germanic way.

The small ending on \textbf{\sk{शुनकः}} is the difference between naming a species and naming the animal at your \sk{द्वारम्}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A dog, in the small friendly form of a very old word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{śunakaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{matsyaḥ}, then \emph{śunakaḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{शुनकः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a dog\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sarpaḥ]{\sk{सर्पः} (sarpaḥ) — a snake}

\label{lesson:SA-C39-snake}



\begin{quote}
Before the last word of the chapter: what did \emph{matsyaḥ} mean, and what did \emph{śunakaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{सर्पः}}
\textbf{\sk{सर्पः}} (\emph{sarpaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a snake\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{सर्पः}} is a snake, named for what it does: \emph{sṛp}, \textquotedblleft{}to creep, to glide\textquotedblright{}.

Latin has the same root, showing up as \emph{serpere}, and \emph{serpent} comes to English straight out of it. \emph{Reptile} arrives by a parallel road from a Latin word meaning much the same thing.

A \textbf{\sk{सर्पः}} belongs in the \sk{तृणम्} rather than on the \sk{शिला}, and that is where the old texts usually put it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five creatures: one in milk, one across the sky, one in the river, one at the door, one in the grass.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sarpaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{dhenuḥ} and \emph{sarpaḥ} together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{सर्पः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a snake\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
